video_title: Active Protection Systems: Protecting Armour In the Drone & Missile Era
gist: Perun traces why hard-kill active protection systems stayed rare for decades across Russia, the US, France, Britain and Germany, and argues drone saturation and the modernisation cycle make APS increasingly necessary despite cost, weight and magazine-depth limits. He treats APS as one layer in a layered defence and frames skipping it as a false economy for forces that expect to fight.

insights.claim: Despite decades of development, most militaries entered 2026 without a hard-kill active protection system fitted as standard to their armour; the barrier was a death of a thousand cuts (cost, weight, power, integration, safety) rather than one fatal flaw.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: APS adoption has been constrained by procurement friction, not technology alone, so budget and integration decisions are the swing factor.
insights.quote: a death of a thousand cuts situation

insights.claim: Hard-kill APS add-ons can cost hundreds of thousands to over a million US dollars per vehicle, add hundreds of kilograms of weight, power and volume demands, and are hardest to integrate on legacy platforms like Abrams, Leopard and Bradley, whose turrets and electrical systems were not designed for them.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Integration cost is lowest on new-design vehicles, favouring new-build programmes over retrofits.

insights.claim: The US Marines evaluating Trophy for Abrams in the mid-2010s cited 2.5 to 3 tons of added weight, transport fit, sea-corrosion risk and a need to harden the radar against small arms and artillery fire.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expeditionary forces face extra APS penalties (weight, corrosion, hardening) beyond those of heavy armour units.

insights.claim: Russia had Arena before 2022 but never funded large-scale rollout; Arena M is only appearing in artisanal numbers, and even new-build T-90M lack it despite thermal camouflage, a remote weapon station and anti-drone protection.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russian armour is largely unprotected by hard-kill APS, limiting the force's survivability in a drone war.

insights.claim: Russia's Afghanit, promised to counter even kinetic APFSDS rounds, was tied to the T-14 Armata; when Armata was deprioritised after the Ukraine invasion for cheaper, mature vehicles, the APS became collateral damage, leaving Arena M as the fallback.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Tying a subsystem to a flagship programme exposes it to the programme's budget fate.

insights.claim: France has run hard-kill APS programmes for over two decades, yet its 2025 order of 100 upgraded Leclerc XLRs has no hard-kill APS; Britain's Challenger 3 plan was 148 tanks but only 60 Trophy kits, roughly one fully equipped regiment.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Even wealthy NATO states under-equip APS, a possible catch-up demand pipeline for vendors like Rafael.
insights.quote: Britain might end up with one tank regiment fully equipped

insights.claim: The US spent decades on APS (Iron Curtain, FCS-era systems, Quick Kill, Raytheon GCV work) without fielding at scale; in 2018 the Army declined to qualify Iron Curtain on Stryker as not mature enough, and it ultimately bought Trophy for Abrams, with Iron Fist on some Bradleys.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Domestic development repeatedly failed, so the US ended up buying proven Israeli systems.

insights.claim: Germany, despite its own hard-kill APS developments, opted to integrate a European version of Trophy on the Leopard 2A8, while the Puma IFV, a 2025 contract for 200 at about EUR4.2 billion (over 20 million per vehicle all-up), has no hard-kill APS.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Trophy is becoming a de facto Western standard; premium vehicles without APS look like a procurement gap.

insights.claim: Soft-kill systems such as the Soviet Shtora are inherently specialised: they only work against specific guidance types from the frontal arc and are vulnerable to seeker adaptations, so hard-kill proved the more robust path.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Defences dependent on a specific sensor type decay as adversaries adapt.

insights.claim: Trophy, first used in combat in 2011 and standard on Israeli Merkava and Namer, was credited in a 2016 US document with Israel losing no tank to anti-armour weapons in 2014 versus Hamas, helping turn hard-kill APS into combat-proven technology.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Combat validation by Israel is what drove Western interest in buying Trophy.

insights.claim: In the 1995 Grozny advance Russia reportedly lost 105 of 120 armoured fighting vehicles, largely to high-angle RPG attacks on thin top armour, which helped motivate Russian hard-kill APS work like Arena.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Top-attack vulnerability in urban fights is a long-standing driver of APS demand.

insights.claim: Battlefield transparency from ISR drones erodes the outer survivability-onion layers (not being seen or hit), so survivability must come from the inner layers of defeating or surviving the hit, which raises APS value.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Rising detection probability shifts defence spending toward hard-kill and protection layers.

insights.claim: Drones require 360-degree and top-hemisphere coverage rather than a frontal cone, and FPV pilots can manoeuvre to hit weak points, while covering vehicles with enough passive armour is impractical.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: APS design requirements shift to all-aspect radar and launchers, raising cost and complexity.

insights.claim: Recognising slow, small drones among clutter is hard: a system tuned to engage fast incoming objects works on RPGs and ATGMs but may misfire on birds or miss a 30 km/h agricultural drone, a problem Perun likens to self-driving cars.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Sensor discrimination, not interceptor performance, may be the key technical bottleneck for anti-drone APS.

insights.claim: Drones are slower and softer than kinetic penetrators, so smaller interceptors suffice; Perun suggests 16 to 20 small drone-optimised interceptors would be preferable to four large ones, and reports that Russia may be increasing Arena M magazine depth with smaller countermeasures.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Magazine depth and cost-per-interceptor become the competitive metrics for next-gen APS.

insights.claim: Tanks and IFVs in Ukraine reportedly take multiple FPV hits to kill, so APS must handle the second, tenth or twentieth drone; footage suggests some Arena M tanks exhausted their countermeasures, and one estimate is an average of about seven successful drone engagements before exhaustion.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: APS buys finite protection, less than a turtle tank absorbing 50 to 60 drones, so it is a complement rather than a replacement.

insights.claim: Both Trophy-equipped Israeli tanks and Arena M-equipped Russian tanks have been lost to small drones, so APS is imperfect.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: APS should be assessed as one probabilistic layer, not a guarantee.

insights.claim: Perun's thesis is that skipping APS is almost always a false economy in the proliferated drone era, except for militaries certain they will never fight; weapons proliferate rather than recede, and 10 to 20 year fleet decisions must assume future drone density.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Supports long-run demand for APS in new vehicle purchases and upgrades.
insights.quote: that's almost always going to be a false economy

insights.claim: Drone threats are cheap and widespread: a Ukrainian Firefly guidance kit for drone-dropped munitions is advertised at about 200 dollars, and drones are used from Syria and Yemen to Myanmar, Africa and cartels.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Low attacker cost and broad proliferation mean even stabilisation missions face drone threats.

insights.claim: Force protection is a layered dice-roll: interceptor drones, short-range gun and missile air defence, C-UAS, RWS, EW, APS and armour each need only stop a share; SHORADs like Pantsir and Tor struggle against FPV-sized targets, and APS covers gaps such as ATGMs and ground-ambush drones.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Layered defence favours integrated sensor and defence suites over single-point solutions.

insights.claim: APS radar costs can be shared with RWS autocannon and C-UAS systems and, with vehicles networked for uncrewed teaming, sensors could pool into a collective picture, creating investment synergies.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Sensor-fusion vendors benefit as APS, C-UAS and networking converge.

insights.claim: Many nations are in a modernisation window (Bradley replacement, European MBT selections, next-gen programmes), which is the cheapest time to integrate APS but also the riskiest for locking in the wrong choice for decades.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: New-design programmes in the next few years will determine APS penetration for decades.

insights.claim: Once vehicles cost eight figures, APS is a smaller marginal cost; for cheaper vehicles, forces may instead choose mobility (US Infantry Squad Vehicle) or standardised peacetime-built cage and up-armour kits, which conflict with hard-kill launchers and sensors.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect a split market: premium APS on expensive platforms, cages and armour kits on cheaper ones.

insights.claim: APS cost comparisons must be holistic: more tanks without APS mean more personnel, depot hours, training and sustainment; and attackers defeating APS-equipped vehicles may need 25 to 50% more munitions per kill, a real constraint where local drone supply is limited.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: APS can raise attacker cost-per-kill and tax scarce local drone stocks.

insights.claim: Perun predicts drones and loitering munitions will become more capable and numerous, and no silver bullet exists; as long as forces commit to mechanised manoeuvre, taking edge off the threat with APS will make economic sense, whereas earlier APS was a luxury when IEDs and mines were the main concern.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for APS and counter-drone spending tied to continued armour investment.
